en.question_text: Which of the following rivers of Madhya Pradesh flows in three states?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Mahi River originates in Madhya Pradesh (from the northern slope of the Vindhya range, near Mhow/Mhau in Dhar district) and flows through three states — Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat — before draining into the Gulf of Khambhat (Arabian Sea). Hence option C (Mahi) is correct.
key_concepts: Ken flows through MP and UP (tributary of Yamuna); Betwa flows through MP and UP (tributary of Yamuna); Sonar is a smaller river.
Mahi is one of the major west-flowing rivers of India (like Narmada and Tapti), originating in MP but crossing into Rajasthan and Gujarat.
MP rivers: Narmada (largest in MP), Tapti, Mahi, Betwa, Ken, Son, Chambal.
Dams on Mahi: Mahi Bajaj Sagar (Rajasthan), Kadana (Gujarat).

Mahi = west-flowing; originates near Mhow, MP.

en.question_text: Which of the following characteristics is not correct in reference to the black soil of Madhya Pradesh?

options.text: Black soil is also known as cotton soil.
Black soil is highly retentive of moisture.
Black soil has high sand content.
Its structure is cloddish but occasionally friable.

explanation.correct_reasoning: Black soil (regur) is clayey, highly retentive of moisture, rich in lime, iron, magnesia and alumina, develops cracks when dry ('self-ploughing'), is known as black cotton soil, and has a cloddish structure. It does NOT have high sand content — that is characteristic of red/sandy soils. Hence option C ('Black soil has high sand content') is the incorrect statement and is correct for this 'not correct' question.

option_explanations.text: Black soil is also known as cotton soil.
Black soil is highly retentive of moisture.
Black soil has high sand content.
Its structure is cloddish but occasionally friable.

key_concepts: Black soil forms from the weathering of basaltic lava rocks (Deccan Trap); found extensively in MP's Narmada valley and Malwa Plateau.
It is fine-grained, clayey, holds moisture well, and is ideal for cotton (hence 'black cotton soil').
High sand content would reduce water retention — opposite of black soil's behaviour; sandy soils are red/yellow soils.
MP-specific: black cotton soil supports cotton in Malwa and Narmada regions.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Not correct about black soil ➜ 'high sand content' (C) — black soil is clayey, not sandy.
For 'not correct' questions, pick the statement opposite to the soil's nature.

en.question_text: Purna river is a tributary of which of the following rivers?

en.question_text: Bijagarh hill is situated in which out of the following mountain ranges?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Bijagarh Hill is situated in the Satpura range. The Satpura mountain range runs east-west across Madhya Pradesh (between the Narmada to the north and Tapti to the south), and Dhupgarh (Pachmarhi) in the Satpura range is the highest point in MP. Hence option A (Satpura range) is correct.
key_concepts: MP's major hill ranges: Satpura (south of Narmada, Dhupgarh highest point ~1,352 m), Vindhya (north of Narmada), Maikal (eastern MP), Mahadeo (part of Satpura, near Pachmarhi/Betul), Kaimur (eastern MP, extending from Bihar).
The Mahadeo hills are often considered the eastern extension of the Satpuras; Bijagarh is associated with the Satpura range in MP geography materials.
Amarkantak (Maikal range) is the source of Narmada and Son.
MPPSC physiography questions frequently test MP hill ranges and their peaks.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Bijagarh Hill ➜ Satpura range (MP).
Satpura = Dhupgarh/Pachmarhi (highest point in MP); Vindhya = north of Narmada.

en.question_text: Which of the following statements is not correct regarding the climate of Madhya Pradesh?

options.text: The climate of Madhya Pradesh is tropical.
The state comes under the monsoon climate.
Temperate climate is found in the southern part of the state.
The Tropic of Cancer passes through its central part.

explanation.correct_reasoning: Madhya Pradesh has a tropical climate and lies within the monsoon (tropical wet-and-dry/savanna) climatic belt; the Tropic of Cancer passes through its central part. A temperate climate is NOT found in the southern part of MP (or anywhere in the state — MP is wholly tropical/subtropical). Hence statement C is not correct, making option C the answer.

option_explanations.text: The climate of Madhya Pradesh is tropical.
The state comes under the monsoon climate.
Temperate climate is found in the southern part of the state.
The Tropic of Cancer passes through its central part.

key_concepts: MP climate: tropical monsoon; three seasons (summer, monsoon, winter); Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) passes through central MP (near Bhopal/Sagar).
Temperate climate occurs in the Himalayan north and the Nilgiri/Peninsular hills at high elevation — not in MP.
Rainfall in MP decreases from east to west; the state receives most rainfall from the Southwest Monsoon.
Not-correct questions: identify the single false statement — here, 'temperate climate in southern MP' is the false one.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: MP climate = tropical monsoon; Tropic of Cancer through central MP; NO temperate climate anywhere in MP.
For 'not correct' questions, pick the statement contradicting the facts.

en.question_text: Which type of forests are not found in Madhya Pradesh?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Madhya Pradesh's forests are mainly tropical moist deciduous (sal, teak), tropical dry deciduous, and thorny/scrub forests in drier areas. Alpine forests occur only in high Himalayan zones (above ~3,000 m) and are NOT found in MP. Hence option D (Alpine forests) is correct.
key_concepts: MP forest types: tropical moist deciduous (eastern MP — Sal), tropical dry deciduous (teak), southern tropical thorn forests; teak is MP's state tree.
Alpine forests: coniferous forests of the Himalayas (deodar, fir, spruce) above the tree line — not found in peninsular MP.
MP forest cover: ~25-27% of geographical area; major national parks (Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Pench, Satpura, Panna) lie in deciduous forest zones.
Vegetation types follow climate: tropical wet deciduous > moist > dry > thorn as rainfall decreases.

MP forests = deciduous (moist/dry) + thorny.

en.question_text: Which of the following thermal power stations is situated at Chachai in Anuppur district?

en.question_text: Which of the following statements is not correct regarding the roadways of Madhya Pradesh according to Basic Road Statistics 2018 - 19?

options.text: The length of the National Highways is more than 8,000 km.
The length of the State Highways is more than 11,000 km.
The length of the District roads is more than 50,000 km.
This state ranks first in the country in road density.

MP does NOT rank first in the country in road density (it ranks well below states/UTs such as Kerala, and its road density is around 15 m/km²) — statement D is not correct. Hence option D is the answer.

The length of the State Highways is more than 11,000 km.
The length of the District roads is more than 50,000 km.
This state ranks first in the country in road density.

en.question_text: In the year 2020 - 21, which of the following districts holds the first position in the production of cotton in Madhya Pradesh?

Hence option B (Khargone) is correct.

Damoh, Mandla and Panna are not leading cotton districts (Panna is known for diamonds; Mandla for forests/tribal population).
MP's cotton production is a small share of India's total (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana lead nationally).
Agriculture questions of this type refer to the MP Economic Survey / agricultural statistics of the cited year.

en.question_text: The Electoral College for the election of the President consists of:

options.text: Members of both houses of Parliament
Members of both houses of Parliament and State Assemblies
Elected members of both houses of Parliament and elected members of State Assemblies

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Electoral College for the election of the President of India (Article 54) consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (including NCT of Delhi and Puducherry). Nominated members are not part of it. Hence option C is correct.

option_explanations.text: Members of both houses of Parliament
Members of both houses of Parliament and State Assemblies
Elected members of both houses of Parliament and elected members of State Assemblies

key_concepts: Article 54: President elected by an electoral college of elected MPs (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha) and elected MLAs of all States + UTs with legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K).
Nominated members (Rajya Sabha, Legislative Councils, Anglo-Indian/nominated MLAs) do NOT vote “elected” is the key word.
Value of each vote is calculated by population formulae (Articles 55, 57); election by proportional representation by means of single transferable vote.
MPPSC polity: distinguish the President's electoral college from that of the Vice-President (both Houses of Parliament only).
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: President's Electoral College = ELECTED MPs + ELECTED MLAs (States + UTs with legislatures).
Nominated members never vote in presidential election.

sources.title: Article 54 — Election of President, Constitution of India

en.question_text: The Directive Principles of State Policy are explained in Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution. This system has been taken from the Constitution of which country?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from the Irish Constitution (they appear in the Irish Constitution as Directive Principles of Social Policy). In the Indian Constitution they are contained in Part IV (Articles 36-51), NOT Part IV-A (which contains Fundamental Duties under Article 51-A). The phrasing 'Part IV-A' in the question is technically incorrect, but the intended question is the source of DPSP — Ireland. Hence option D is correct.
key_concepts: Sources of the Indian Constitution: parliamentary system & rule of law (Britain), Fundamental Rights (USA), DPSP (Ireland), emergency provisions (Germany/Weimar), federal scheme (Canada/Government of India Act 1935), Fundamental Duties (USSR).
DPSP = Articles 36-51 (Part IV); non-justiciable, fundamental in governance; Article 37 makes them fundamental in governance but not enforceable by courts.
Part IV-A (Article 51-A, added by 42nd Amendment, 1976) = Fundamental Duties — do not confuse with Part IV DPSP.
Question-wording note: the statement 'DPSP are explained in Part IV-A' is inaccurate; correct location is Part IV.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: DPSP ➜ Ireland (source); Part IV, Articles 36-51 (location). Part IV-A = Fundamental Duties.
Exam trap: never confuse DPSP (Part IV) with Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A).

sources.title: Directive Principles of State Policy — Articles 36-51

en.question_text: The Parliament is formed by which of the following?

options.text: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and President
Prime Minister, Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha

explanation.correct_reasoning: Under Article 79 of the Constitution, the Parliament of India consists of the President and the two Houses — the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha). Hence option C (Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and President) is correct.

option_explanations.text: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and President
Prime Minister, Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha

key_concepts: Article 79: 'There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People.'
The President is an integral part of Parliament (summons, prorogues, dissolves Lok Sabha, gives assent to bills) but is not a member of either House.
The Prime Minister is not a constitutional component of Parliament (though a member of Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha).
Distinct from State Legislature (Article 168): Governor + Legislative Assembly (+ Legislative Council where it exists).
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Parliament of India = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha (Article 79).
President is part of Parliament; PM is not a separate constitutional component.

en.question_text: When was NABARD established?

en.question_text: How many banks were nationalized in India in 1980?

en.question_text: Through which Amendment of the Constitution has the Right to Education become a Fundamental Right?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Right to Education became a Fundamental Right under Article 21-A through the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002. It made free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years a Fundamental Right; the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 followed to implement it. Hence option D (Eighty-sixth Constitutional Amendment) is correct.
key_concepts: 86th Amendment, 2002: inserted Article 21-A (right to education), modified Article 45 (early childhood care), and added Article 51A(k) (11th Fundamental Duty — parent/guardian to provide education to child aged 6-14).
RTE Act, 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010.
42nd Amendment (1976) = mini-Constitution; 44th Amendment (1978) = rolled back Emergency provisions; 1st Amendment (1951) = land reform/Schedule 9.
MPPSC polity: amendment-number associations are frequently tested.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Right to Education = Article 21-A ➜ 86th Amendment, 2002 (RTE Act 2009).
Age group: 6-14 years; free and compulsory.

en.question_text: By which Constitutional Amendment was the term 'Socialist' included in the Preamble?

en.question_text: Bhima Nayak was related to which Princely State?

en.question_text: Which folk dance is prevalent on the occasion of Diwali in the regional areas of Sagar?

en.question_text: Whose famous literary work is 'Mukul'?

en.question_text: Nohdora ornamentation made of clay on the wall is the speciality of which tribe?

en.question_text: Where is the historical Matangeshwar temple situated?

en.question_text: Whose famous work is Ramchandrika?

en.question_text: On whom did Balkrishna Sharma Naveen write two kavyas—Tranarpan and Atmosarga?

Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi (1890-1931): founder-editor of Hindi newspaper 'Pratap', Kanpur; martyr of communal harmony — killed while rescuing people during Kanpur riots, 25 March 1931.
Pranarpan and Atmosarga are literary tributes to Vidyarthi's sacrifice.

en.question_text: In human beings, disorder caused due to trisomy of 21st chromosome is:

explanation.correct_reasoning: Down syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome 21, i.e. the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21). The condition was first clinically described by John Langdon Down in 1866, and its chromosomal basis was established by Jerome Lejeune in 1959. It is the most common chromosomal disorder in humans and causes characteristic physical features with intellectual disability. Hence option B is correct.
key_concepts: Turner syndrome = monosomy X (45,X), affects females only (missing/partial X chromosome).
Super female syndrome = trisomy X (47,XXX), an extra X chromosome in females.
Klinefelter syndrome = 47,XXY, an extra X chromosome in males.
None of Turner, Super Female or Klinefelter involves chromosome 21; all are sex-chromosome aneuploidies.
Down syndrome risk rises with maternal age; incidence roughly 1 in 700–1,000 live births.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Trisomy 21 = Down syndrome. Think chromosome '21' ➜ 'Down'.
All other options are sex-chromosome (X/Y) disorders, not chromosome-21 disorders.

sources.title: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Principles of Inheritance and Variation (chromosomal disorders)
MedlinePlus Genetics – Down Syndrome (trisomy 21)

en.question_text: National Health Policy 2017 identified coordinated action on seven priority areas for improving health. Which option is not included under the seven priority areas?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The National Health Policy (NHP) 2017 aims at universal health coverage and calls for coordinated action in seven priority areas to improve the health environment: (1) Swachh Bharat Abhiyan; (2) balanced, healthy diets and regular exercise; (3) addressing tobacco, alcohol and substance abuse; (4) Yatri Suraksha — preventing deaths due to rail and road traffic accidents; (5) Nirbhaya Nari — action against gender violence; (6) reduced stress and improved safety at the workplace; (7) reducing indoor and outdoor air pollution. The Annapurna Scheme (food security for eligible senior citizens not covered by an old-age pension) is a social-welfare/food-security scheme and is NOT one of these seven health priority areas. Hence option D is correct.
key_concepts: NHP 2017 succeeded the National Health Policies of 1983 and 2002.
Aspirational goal: raise government health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 2025.
Annapurna Scheme was launched on 1 April 2000 to provide food security to senior citizens eligible for but not receiving an old-age pension.
The seven NHP 2017 areas are coordinated cross-sectoral actions, not a list of all health schemes.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Annapurna = food for the aged (welfare), whereas NHP 2017's seven areas are health-environment actions — Annapurna does not belong.
The odd one out is Annapurna Scheme (D).

en.question_text: Which pulse causes lathyrism when consumed on a regular basis?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Lathyrism is a neuroparalytic disorder (spastic paraparesis of the lower limbs) caused by chronic excessive consumption of khesari dal (grass pea, Lathyrus sativus). Khesari dal contains the neurotoxic amino acid beta-N-oxalylamino-L-alanine (BOAA, also called ODAP). Prolonged consumption damages upper motor neurons, leading to muscle weakness and paralysis of the legs. Hence option A is correct.
key_concepts: Chana dal (chickpea) and moong dal (green gram) do not contain BOAA and do not cause lathyrism.
The Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) has developed low-BOAA khesari strains through tissue-culture/breeding work.
Lathyrism is prevalent where khesari dal is a dietary staple — parts of Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Bangladesh and Ethiopia.
MP connection: 'lokhand' (lathyrism) is a recognized public-health concern in khesari-consuming belts of Madhya Pradesh.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Khesari dal ➜ BOAA toxin ➜ Lathyrism (leg paralysis).
Think 'K' for Khesari and 'L' for Lathyrism.

sources.title: National Institute of Nutrition / ICMR — Khesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) and BOAA neurolathyrism

en.question_text: In 2017, which Satellite Launch Vehicle of ISRO successfully launched 104 satellites in a single flight?

The primary payload was Cartosat-2 Series, accompanied by 103 nano/international satellites. Hence option D is correct.

INSAT-3DR is an advanced meteorological/communication satellite, not a 104-satellite mission.
PSLV-C55 (2023) and GSLV-F12 (2023) are different, later missions.

en.question_text: Ozone layer thickness is measured in:

explanation.correct_reasoning: The thickness (total column amount) of the ozone layer is measured in Dobson Units (DU), named after G. M. B. Dobson. One DU corresponds to a layer of pure ozone 0.01 mm thick at standard temperature and pressure. Normal values are around 300 DU; readings below about 220 DU define an 'ozone hole'. Hence option B is correct.
key_concepts: Decibels measure sound intensity, not ozone.
PPB (parts per billion) and PPM (parts per million) express gas concentrations, not total column ozone thickness.
Ozone is measured with Dobson spectrophotometers and by satellite instruments such as TOMS/OMI.
The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV-B and UV-C radiation; the Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Ozone thickness ➜ Dobson Units (DU). Think 'D' for Dobson and 'Ozone'.
Do not confuse DU (total column ozone) with PPB/PPM (trace-gas concentration).

sources.title: NASA Ozone Watch — Dobson Unit

en.question_text: The number of cervical vertebrae in a human body is:

explanation.correct_reasoning: A human vertebral column has 7 cervical vertebrae (C1–C7) in the neck region. This number is remarkably constant across mammals — even a giraffe has only 7 cervical vertebrae. C1 is the atlas and C2 is the axis. Hence option B is correct.
key_concepts: The adult vertebral column has 33 vertebrae in all: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral (fused into sacrum) and 4 coccygeal (fused into coccyx).
Option D's '33' is the total number of vertebrae, not the cervical count (and the trailing '2' appears to be a printing artifact).
Cervical vertebrae are the smallest and most mobile vertebrae and support the skull.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: 7 cervical vertebrae — '7 in the neck' (C1 atlas, C2 axis).
Recall the full count as 7-12-5-5-4 (cervical-thoracic-lumbar-sacral-coccygeal).

en.question_text: In which year was India's first interplanetary mission to planet Mars launched successfully?

India succeeded in its very first attempt to Mars, and the mission was notably cost-effective (around ₹450 crore).
The launch vehicle was PSLV-C25 (not GSLV), because MOM was a relatively light spacecraft.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: MOM/Mangalyaan launched 5 November 2013 (PSLV-C25); Mars orbit reached 24 September 2014.
First interplanetary = Mars; year = 2013.

en.question_text: When did the Government of India pass the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted by Parliament in 1974. It was India's first major environmental legislation, aimed at preventing and controlling water pollution and maintaining/restoring the wholesomeness of water. It also led to the constitution of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs). Hence option D (1974) is correct.

The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act came in 1981; the Environment (Protection) Act came in 1986 (after the Bhopal gas tragedy).
CPCB was constituted in 1974 under the Water Act.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Water Act = 1974 — India's first major environmental law; it created CPCB and SPCBs.
Sequence: Water Act 1974 → Air Act 1981 → Environment Protection Act 1986.

en.question_text: According to SDG India Index 2018, SDG1, SDG2, and SDG9 represent respectively:

options.text: No poverty; Zero hunger; Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure
No poverty; Quality education; Life on land
Clean water and sanitation; Climate action; Sustainable cities and communities
Gender equality; Climate action; Zero hunger

explanation.correct_reasoning: Under the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by the UN in 2015: SDG 1 = No Poverty; SDG 2 = Zero Hunger; SDG 9 = Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure. Hence option A is correct.

option_explanations.text: No poverty; Zero hunger; Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure
No poverty; Quality education; Life on land
Clean water and sanitation; Climate action; Sustainable cities and communities
Gender equality; Climate action; Zero hunger

key_concepts: SDG 4 = Quality Education; SDG 5 = Gender Equality; SDG 6 = Clean Water and Sanitation; SDG 13 = Climate Action; SDG 11 = Sustainable Cities and Communities; SDG 15 = Life on Land.
There are 17 SDGs and 169 targets, with a target year of 2030.
India tracks SDG progress through the NITI Aayog SDG India Index.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: SDG 1–2–9 = No Poverty – Zero Hunger – Industry/Innovation/Infrastructure.
Match each SDG number to its title; option A is the only one with all three correct.

sources.title: United Nations — Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
NITI Aayog — SDG India Index

en.question_text: In the aquatic ecosystem of a pond, which of the following components is represented by fungi, bacteria, and flagellates?

explanation.correct_reasoning: In a pond (aquatic) ecosystem, fungi and bacteria act as decomposers (saprotrophs). They secrete enzymes onto dead organic matter (dead plants and animals), break it down into simpler inorganic substances, and release the nutrients back into the soil/water for reuse by producers. Hence option C is correct.
key_concepts: Autotrophs (producers) = green plants and algae that make their own food by photosynthesis.
Consumers = herbivores, carnivores and omnivores that eat other organisms.
Abiotic components = non-living factors such as light, temperature, water and dissolved nutrients.
Decomposers complete nutrient cycling in an ecosystem.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Fungi and bacteria = nature's recyclers = decomposers (saprotrophs).
Dead matter ➜ fungi/bacteria ➜ nutrients returned to producers.

sources.title: NCERT Class 12 Biology, Ecosystem (ecosystem components: producers, consumers, decomposers)

en.question_text: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court of India declare the prevalence of Fundamental Rights over Directive Principles of the State Policy in case of conflict between the two?

options.text: The State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
Kesavananda Bharati v. the State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. the Union of India (1980)

explanation.correct_reasoning: In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Supreme Court of India held that Fundamental Rights would prevail over the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in the event of a conflict, because Fundamental Rights are justiciable/enforceable by courts while DPSPs are non-justiciable. This conflict and its resolution directly led to the First Constitutional Amendment (1951). Hence option B is correct.

option_explanations.text: The State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
Kesavananda Bharati v. the State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. the Union of India (1980)

key_concepts: Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot curtail Fundamental Rights.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): introduced the 'basic structure' doctrine.
Minerva Mills (1980): restored balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs; declared judicial review part of basic structure.
The 1951 Champakam judgment prompted the First Amendment (Articles 15(4), 31A/31B and the Ninth Schedule).
FR vs DPSP hierarchy: FRs are enforceable; DPSPs are directive but not enforceable by courts.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) ➜ Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSP ➜ led to First Amendment (1951).
It is the earliest of the four cases listed and the one that resolved FR-vs-DPSP precedence first.

sources.title: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) — Supreme Court of India

en.question_text: Which one of the following statements is not correct?

options.text: In case of differences of opinion amongst the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners, the matter is decided by the Law Commission.
The Election Commissioners cannot be removed from their office except on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.
The Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners enjoy equal powers.
The term of office of Election Commissioners is six years from the date they assume office or till the day they attain the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.

explanation.correct_reasoning: The question asks which statement about the Election Commission of India is NOT correct. Option A is incorrect: differences of opinion among the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners are decided by the Election Commission itself (by majority), not by the Law Commission. Since A is the false statement, it is the answer to a 'not correct' question. Hence option A is correct.

option_explanations.text: In case of differences of opinion amongst the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners, the matter is decided by the Law Commission.
The Election Commissioners cannot be removed from their office except on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.
The Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners enjoy equal powers.
The term of office of Election Commissioners is six years from the date they assume office or till the day they attain the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.

key_concepts: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission.
CEC and other ECs have equal powers; decisions are by majority.
CEC can be removed like a Supreme Court judge; other ECs can be removed only on the CEC's recommendation (Article 324(5)).
Term: six years or age 65, whichever is earlier. The Law Commission is a legal-reform body, not an electoral-dispute authority.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: EC differences decided by the Commission (majority), NOT the Law Commission — so A is the 'not correct' statement.
For 'not correct' questions, pick the statement that is factually false.

sources.title: Article 324 and the Election Commission (Conditions of Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991

en.question_text: An amendment of the Constitution shall require to be ratified by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the states:

options.text: If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 53.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 239A.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 243A.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 279A.

explanation.correct_reasoning: Under the proviso to Article 368(2), certain constitutional amendments require, in addition to a special majority in Parliament, ratification by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States. Article 279A (which constitutes the GST Council) was added to this mandatory-ratification list by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, so any change to Article 279A needs both a special majority and ratification by at least half the state legislatures. Hence option D is correct.

option_explanations.text: If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 53.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 239A.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 243A.
If such amendment seeks to make changes in Article 279A.

key_concepts: Other ratification-triggering provisions: election of the President (Arts 54, 55), extent of executive power (Arts 73, 74), judiciary (Arts 124–147, 214–231), High Courts for states, the Seventh Schedule, representation of states in Parliament, and Article 368 itself.
Articles 53 (Union executive power), 239A and 243A (local bodies) are not in this mandatory half-state ratification list.
Half of the states means roughly 14–15 state legislatures must pass resolutions ratifying the amendment before the President's assent.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Article 279A (GST Council) — changes need special majority + ratification by half the state legislatures (101st Amendment, 2016).
Ratification = federal feature protecting state interests.

sources.title: Article 368, Constitution of India; 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 (GST)

en.question_text: Which among the following articles speaks about impeachment of the President of India?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Article 61 of the Constitution lays down the procedure for the impeachment of the President of India for 'violation of the Constitution'. The charge may be preferred in either House of Parliament, requires signatures of one-fourth of its members, must be passed by a two-thirds majority of the total membership of that House, is then investigated by the other House, and if sustained by a two-thirds majority, results in the President's removal. Hence option C (Article 61) is correct.
key_concepts: Article 60 = President's oath/affirmation; Article 62 = time of election to fill vacancy and term; Article 63 = Vice-President of India.
Impeachment is a quasi-judicial, parliamentary process; the only ground is 'violation of the Constitution'.
No President of India has ever been impeached.
The nominated members of Parliament also take part in the impeachment process.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Impeachment of the President ➜ Article 61.
Articles 60 (oath), 62 (vacancy), 63 (Vice-President) are the nearby distractors.

sources.title: Article 61, Constitution of India (Procedure for impeachment of the President)

en.question_text: As per Article 76 of the Indian Constitution, the President shall appoint a person to be Attorney General for India:

options.text: who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the High Court.
who has been an advocate of the Supreme Court for at least seven years.
who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court.
who has been an advocate of the High Court for at least seven years.

explanation.correct_reasoning: Article 76 of the Constitution provides for the Attorney General for India, who is appointed by the President and must be a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court (i.e., a citizen of India who has been a judge of a High Court for at least five years, or an advocate of a High Court/Supreme Court for at least ten years, or is in the President's opinion an eminent jurist). Hence option C is correct.

option_explanations.text: who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the High Court.
who has been an advocate of the Supreme Court for at least seven years.
who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court.
who has been an advocate of the High Court for at least seven years.

key_concepts: The Attorney General is the highest law officer of India and advises the Government of India on legal matters.
He/She has the right of audience in all courts in India and can participate in Parliament proceedings but cannot vote.
The Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President and is not a member of the Cabinet (unlike in some other systems).
Qualification threshold is Supreme Court-judge level, not High Court-judge level.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Attorney General (Article 76) ➜ qualified to be a Supreme Court Judge.
AG = highest law officer; SC-judge qualification; right of audience in all courts.

sources.title: Article 76, Constitution of India (Attorney General for India)

en.question_text: K.M. Munshi was related to:

explanation.correct_reasoning: K. M. Munshi (Kanhaiyalal Maneklal Munshi) was a member of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, which was chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. He was also a freedom fighter, lawyer and the founder of Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan. Hence option B (Constitution Draft Committee) is correct.
key_concepts: The Drafting Committee had seven members: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar (chairman), K. M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Iyer, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Syed Mohammad Saadulla, B. L. Mitter and D. P. Khaitan.
The Public Accounts Committee is a parliamentary financial committee (not a Constituent Assembly body).
The Preamble was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru (Objectives Resolution, 1946); there was no separate 'Preamble Committee' headed by Munshi.
The Hindu Code Bill was associated mainly with Dr. Ambedkar as Law Minister, not with Munshi's Constituent Assembly role.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: K. M. Munshi ➜ member of the Drafting Committee (chaired by Dr. Ambedkar).
Drafting Committee = 7 members; Munshi was one of them.

sources.title: Constituent Assembly of India — Drafting Committee members
sources.citation: Constitution of India / Parliament of India

en.question_text: Under whose advice can the President of India declare Emergency under Article 352?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Under Article 352 of the Constitution, the President may proclaim a National Emergency only on the written advice of the Union Cabinet (the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 made the Cabinet's written advice mandatory, so the President cannot act on the Prime Minister's advice alone). Hence option C (Union Cabinet) is correct.
key_concepts: Article 352 grounds: war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
The proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month (by special majority) and remains in force for six months, extendable.
'Council of Ministers' is broader than the 'Union Cabinet'; the Constitution specifically requires the Cabinet's written advice for an emergency proclamation.
The 44th Amendment (1978) also replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' to prevent misuse.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: National Emergency (Article 352) ➜ President acts on the Union Cabinet's written advice (44th Amendment).
Not the PM alone — it is the Cabinet.

sources.title: Article 352, Constitution of India (Proclamation of Emergency); 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978

en.question_text: The Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Good Governance and Policy Analysis is in:

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Good Governance and Policy Analysis (AIGGPA), formerly the School of Good Governance and Policy Analysis, is located in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. It was set up by the Madhya Pradesh Government in September 2007 and functions at Sushasan Bhawan, Bhopal. Hence option C (Bhopal) is correct; the earlier key of New Delhi was factually wrong and contradicted the question's own explanation.

option_explanations.reason: New Delhi hosts other policy institutes, but not this one.
Hyderabad is not the seat of this institute.
Correct. The Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Good Governance and Policy Analysis is located in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
Jabalpur is not the seat of this institute.

key_concepts: AIGGPA is an autonomous think-tank of the Government of Madhya Pradesh for policy analysis, governance research and training (e-governance, citizen-centric services).
It is distinct from national institutions located in Delhi such as the Lokpal or IIPA.
MP connection: it supports the MP state government in formulating and implementing policy frameworks.
The institute's address is Sushasan Bhawan, Bhadbhada Chouraha, Bhopal.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: AIGGPA (good governance institute) ➜ Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
Answer key correction: New Delhi (A) was wrong; correct answer is Bhopal (C).

sources.title: Atal Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Good Governance and Policy Analysis (AIGGPA), Bhopal

en.question_text: The Brahmi script used in the Ashokan edicts was first deciphered in 1837 by:

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Brahmi script used in the Ashokan edicts was first deciphered in 1837 by James Prinsep, an East India Company officer and antiquary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal. By comparing Brahmi inscriptions with the better-known Kharosthi script and bilingual coins, Prinsep unlocked the reading of Ashoka's edicts, which revealed the Mauryan emperor's Dhamma. Hence option B (James Prinsep) is correct.
key_concepts: James Prinsep also deciphered the Kharosthi script and founded the field of Indian epigraphy/numismatics.
Alexander Cunningham founded the Archaeological Survey of India (1861); John Marshall excavated Indus sites and Sanchi; William Jones founded the Asiatic Society (1784) and championed Sanskrit.
Brahmi is the ancestor of most modern Indian scripts; Ashokan edicts were written in Brahmi (Prakrit) across the Mauryan empire.
The decipherment (1837) is a landmark in understanding ancient Indian history.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Brahmi script deciphered 1837 ➜ James Prinsep.
Prinsep = Brahmi & Kharosthi; Cunningham = ASI; Jones = Asiatic Society; Marshall = Indus/Sanchi.

sources.title: James Prinsep and the decipherment of Brahmi — Asiatic Society / Indian epigraphy

en.question_text: The list of powers, authority and responsibilities which may be entrusted to the Panchayats is given in the:

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Eleventh Schedule of the Constitution, added by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992), lists 29 functions/matters (e.g., agriculture, land improvement, minor irrigation, animal husbandry, primary education, health and sanitation) that may be entrusted to Panchayats (rural local bodies) by state legislatures. Hence option A (Eleventh Schedule) is correct.
key_concepts: Twelfth Schedule (74th Amendment, 1992) lists 18 functions for Municipalities (urban local bodies) — not Panchayats.
Seventh Schedule divides powers between Centre and States (Union, State, Concurrent Lists).
'State list' is one of the lists in the Seventh Schedule, not the schedule of Panchayat functions.
The 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayats (Part IX, Article 243); the 74th did the same for Municipalities.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Panchayats ➜ Eleventh Schedule (73rd Amendment, 1992, 29 functions); Municipalities ➜ Twelfth Schedule (74th Amendment).
Rural = Eleventh; Urban = Twelfth.

sources.title: 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 — Eleventh Schedule (Panchayats)

en.question_text: Bhimma tribe lives in which of the districts of Madhya Pradesh ?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Bhimma (also written Bhoomia) tribe is a Scheduled Tribe community of Madhya Pradesh that is primarily found in Mandla and Dindori districts, both tribal-dominated districts in the eastern part of the state. The Bhimma are listed in the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950. Hence option B (Mandla and Dindori) is correct.
key_concepts: Betul and Chhindwara are better known for Gond and Baiga populations.
Rewa-Satna and Sidhi-Shahdol lie in the Baghelkhand belt, with different predominant tribal communities.
Madhya Pradesh has the largest Scheduled Tribe population among Indian states; Mandla and Dindori are among its tribal-majority districts.
The Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950 is the authoritative list of ST communities.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Bhimma tribe ➜ Mandla & Dindori (eastern tribal belt of MP).
Pair each MP tribe with its home district — a frequent MPPSC pattern.

sources.title: Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950 — Ministry of Tribal Affairs, GoI

en.question_text: Mandwara festival is celebrated by the :

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Mandwara festival is celebrated by the Gonds, one of the largest tribal groups in Central India and Madhya Pradesh. Festivals are a key marker of tribal identity in MP, and Mandwara is specifically associated with the Gond community. Hence option A (Gonds) is correct.
key_concepts: Gonds are the largest tribe in Madhya Pradesh; the Gondwana region is named after them.
Baigas are mainly found in Mandla, Balaghat, Dindori and Shahdol; Bhariyas and Sahariyas have their own distinct festivals and regions.
Other well-known MP tribal festivals include Bhagoria (Bhil) and Bhujalia.
MPPSC frequently tests tribe–festival pairings.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Mandwara festival ➜ Gonds.
Learn MP tribe–district–festival triplets together.

sources.title: MP Tribal Affairs — Scheduled Tribes of Madhya Pradesh

en.question_text: Mahanayak Tantya Mama is related to which tribal group?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Mahanayak Tantya Mama, popularly known as Tantia Bhil or Tantya Bhil, was a Bhil tribal freedom fighter who led an armed resistance against the British in the Nimar and western Madhya Pradesh region during the late 19th century. He is revered as a tribal hero (sometimes called the 'Robin Hood of MP'). Hence option C (Bhil) is correct.
key_concepts: Tantya Bhil operated mainly in the Nimar region (Khandwa, Khargone, Barwani) and was captured and hanged by the British.
Kol, Gond and Bhariya are distinct tribes of MP with their own leaders and histories.
Tantya Mama is commemorated in MP through schemes, monuments and the Tantya Mama Economic Welfare Scheme.
His resistance is part of the tribal freedom-struggle narrative of MP.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Tantya Mama = Tantia Bhil ➜ Bhil tribe.
Name itself gives the tribe: Tantya 'Bhil'.

sources.title: Madhya Pradesh tribal freedom fighters — Tantya Bhil/Tantya Mama

en.question_text: Freedom fighter Raghunath Singh Mandloi is related to the:

explanation.correct_reasoning: Raghunath Singh Mandloi was a freedom fighter belonging to the Bhilala tribe, from Barwani district of Madhya Pradesh. He actively participated in the Revolt of 1857 against the British in the Nimar region. Hence option B (Bhilala tribe) is correct.
key_concepts: The Bhilala tribe is concentrated in western MP — Jhabua, Alirajpur, Dhar and Barwani districts.
Raghunath Singh Mandloi's role is tied to the 1857 revolt in the Nimar/Barwani area.
Korkus are mainly in Betul, Harda and Khandwa; Baigas in Mandla-Balaghat-Dindori — different from Mandloi's Bhilala identity.
MPPSC often links 1857 rebel leaders of MP to their tribe and district.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Raghunath Singh Mandloi ➜ Bhilala tribe, Barwani, 1857 revolt.
All options are MP tribes — match the leader to the correct one.

sources.title: Freedom fighters of Madhya Pradesh — Revolt of 1857 in MP

en.question_text: Who is late Shri Badal Bhoi?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Shri Badal Bhoi was a famous tribal freedom fighter from Dungria Titra village, Parasia tehsil (Chhindwara district), Madhya Pradesh. Born in 1845, he led tribal resistance against British rule. Hence option C (Famous tribal freedom fighter) is correct.
key_concepts: Badal Bhoi's resistance was centred in the Parasia–Chhindwara area of MP.
The other options describe different kinds of tribal contribution; Badal Bhoi is specifically remembered as a freedom fighter.
MP honours its tribal freedom fighters (Badal Bhoi, Tantya Bhil, Raghunath Singh Mandloi, Shankar Shah–Raghunath Shah) in its freedom-struggle narrative.
Parasia is in Chhindwara district, a region with significant Gond and other tribal population.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Badal Bhoi ➜ tribal freedom fighter, Dungria Titra, Parasia (Chhindwara).
Born 1845 — a pre-1857/1857-era tribal resister of British rule in MP.

sources.title: Tribal freedom fighters of Madhya Pradesh

en.question_text: Which award is given to women for tribal, folk, and traditional arts by the Madhya Pradesh Government?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The National Devi Ahilya Award is conferred by the Madhya Pradesh Government to recognise the creativity of women artists in tribal, folk and traditional arts. It was instituted in 1996–97 and is named after Rani Ahilyabai Holkar of Maheshwar. Hence option C (National Devi Ahilya Award) is correct.
key_concepts: National Kabir Award — given by MP for contributions in the field of communal harmony / saint-poet Kabir's philosophy (different field).
Shikhar Award and Tulsi Award are other MP honours with different specific purposes.
Rani Ahilyabai Holkar ruled Maheshwar (Maheshwar, Khargone district) and is celebrated for governance and temple-building.
The award specifically targets women artists working in tribal/folk/traditional art forms — an MP-specific cultural honour.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Devi Ahilya Award ➜ women artists, tribal/folk/traditional arts (MP).
Named after Rani Ahilyabai Holkar; instituted 1996-97.

en.question_text: Birha is the popular folk song of which group of tribal women?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Birha is a traditional folk song (and dance) form associated with the Gond tribe, particularly of the Baghelkhand region of Madhya Pradesh. Hence option A (Gond) is correct.
key_concepts: Baghelkhand covers eastern MP districts such as Satna, Rewa, Sidhi and Shahdol, where Gonds are prominent.
Kol, Bhil and Sahariya each have their own distinct folk songs and dances.
Folk forms are a common MPPSC MP-culture topic — tribe–form pairings recur.
Birha expresses themes of separation, longing and daily life.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Birha folk song ➜ Gond tribe, Baghelkhand region.
Baghelkhand = eastern MP (Satna, Rewa, Sidhi, Shahdol).

options.text: Veer Shankar Shah - Raghunath Shah National Award

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Veer Shankar Shah – Raghunath Shah National Award is given by the Madhya Pradesh Government for writings on the cultural tradition and specialties of tribal life in Indian literature. Shankar Shah and Raghunath Shah were Gond rulers of Jabalpur who led the Revolt of 1857 in the region and were executed by the British. Hence option B is correct.

Rani Durgavati Award — named after the Gond queen of Garha-Mandla who fought the Mughals.
Devi Ahilya Award — women artists in tribal/folk/traditional arts (Q26).

en.question_text: In whose name is the Self-Employment Scheme being run for tribals in Madhya Pradesh?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The self-employment scheme for tribals in Madhya Pradesh is the 'Bhagwan Birsa Munda Self-Employment Scheme' (Bhagwan Birsa Munda Swarozgar Yojana), launched by the MP Government on 6 September 2022 in a cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan. It is named after the legendary tribal freedom fighter Birsa Munda. Hence option C (Birsa Munda) is correct. Option B (Tantya Bhil) refers to a different scheme — the Tantya Mama Economic Welfare Scheme — so it is not the answer to *this* question.

option_explanations.reason: Dalpati Shah is not the name of the scheme.
Tantya Mama is a separate MP scheme (Tantya Mama Aarthik Kalyan Yojana) aimed at BPL tribal families, not this self-employment scheme.
Correct. The Bhagwan Birsa Munda Self-Employment Scheme (Swarojgar Yojana) is the MP scheme for tribal self-employment, approved on 6 September 2022.
Raghunath Shah is a historical figure of Garha Mandla, not the name of this scheme.

key_concepts: Under the scheme, projects of ₹1–50 lakh (manufacturing) and ₹1–25 lakh (service/business) are supported; family income ceiling ₹12 lakh; 5% interest subsidy for up to 7 years.
Tantya Bhil is honoured through the separate Tantya Mama Economic Welfare Scheme (smaller projects, ₹10,000–₹1 lakh).
Dalpati Shah and Raghunath Shah are figures associated with the 1857 revolt in MP (Gond rulers of Garha-Mandla/Jabalpur region), not with this self-employment scheme.
The scheme is implemented through the MP Adivasi Finance and Development Corporation.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Tribal self-employment scheme (MP) ➜ Bhagwan Birsa Munda, launched 6 Sept 2022.
Do not confuse with Tantya Mama scheme (Tantya Bhil) — they are two different tribal schemes.

sources.title: Approval of Bhagwan Birsa Munda Self-Employment Scheme, MP cabinet 6 September 2022

en.question_text: What was the lower ceiling of the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) which was amended in 2007 by the Government of India?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is the percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that banks must maintain in liquid assets (cash, gold, approved securities). Until 2007, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 prescribed a lower ceiling (floor) of 25% for SLR. The 2007 amendment removed this 25% lower ceiling, giving the RBI flexibility to prescribe SLR within a band. Hence option B (25%) is correct.
key_concepts: SLR is a monetary-tool reserve; CRR is the cash portion kept with RBI (no interest), while SLR assets earn some return.
After 2007, RBI sets SLR; current SLR is 18% (as of recent policy), showing the downward flexibility gained after the floor was removed.
The 25% figure is the statutory lower ceiling that existed before 2007 — the precise fact being tested.
MPPSC economy questions often test statutory floors/ceilings removed or retained by amendments.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: SLR lower ceiling before 2007 = 25%; removed by Banking Regulation Act amendment 2007.
SLR vs CRR: SLR = liquid assets with the bank itself; CRR = cash with RBI.

sources.title: Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — Statutory Liquidity Ratio; Reserve Bank of India

en.question_text: In which of the following irrigation projects do four states have a partnership?

en.question_text: What is the name of the author of the historical novel Durgesh Nandini written in Bengali language?

en.question_text: Who appointed Keshav Chandra Sen as the Chief Acharya of Brahmo Samaj?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Keshav Chandra Sen was appointed Chief Acharya of the Brahmo Samaj by Debendranath Tagore (also written Devendranath Thakur), who had joined the Brahmo Samaj in 1842 and was its leader. en.question_text: During which movement did Gandhiji call for a boycott of the Prince of Wales?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Mahatma Gandhi called for a boycott of the Prince of Wales (later Edward VIII) during his visit to India in 1921, as part of the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22). The boycott was part of the wider programme of surrendering titles, boycotting courts, schools and foreign goods. Hence option B (Non-Cooperation Movement) is correct.

The Non-Cooperation Movement was suspended after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922).
The Prince of Wales visit (Nov 1921) was greeted with hartals and boycotts.

en.question_text: In the administrative system of the Mauryan period, Pradeshta is related to which department?

explanation.correct_reasoning: In the Mauryan administrative system, the Pradeshta was connected with the judiciary/justice department. The Pradeshika was the district administrator, while the Pradeshta functioned in the judicial sphere. Hence option B (Justice Department) is correct.
key_concepts: Mauryan administration (from Kautilya's Arthashastra and Megasthenes): the empire was divided into provinces, districts and villages; officials included Pradeshika (district head), Yukta, and Pradeshta (judicial).
Revenue was handled by officials such as the Samaharta (collector-general) and Sannidhata (treasurer).
Military was under the Senapati and a war board with six sub-committees (per Megasthenes).
The Pradeshta's judicial role distinguishes it from the revenue and military arms.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Mauryan Pradeshta ➜ Justice (judicial) department.
Pradeshika = district administrator; Pradeshta = judicial — similar names, different roles.

en.question_text: For whom did K.M. Panikkar says that "He was the first diplomat of modern India"?

Pannikar), the historian and diplomat, described Gopal Krishna Gokhale as 'the first diplomat of modern India' for his measured, constitutional approach and his role in presenting India's case to the British. en.question_text: In which Vedas are Sabha and Samiti included as separate institutions?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Atharvaveda mentions the Sabha and Samiti as two distinct institutions and refers to them as the 'daughters of Prajapati' (the creator), reflecting their importance in Vedic polity as assemblies. Hence option C (Atharvaveda) is correct.
key_concepts: Sabha and Samiti were Vedic popular assemblies (Sabha = council of elders/nobles; Samiti = broader assembly of the people) involved in governance and electing chiefs.
The Rigveda also mentions them but the Atharvaveda explicitly treats them as two separate institutions/daughters of Prajapati — the standard textbook answer for this phrasing.
Later, with the rise of kingship, these assemblies lost prominence.
This is a standard ancient-history fact tested in MPSC/UPSC-style prelims.

Vedic assemblies: Sabha (council) and Samiti (people's assembly).

en.question_text: There was a provision for reciting which mantra in the Upanayana ritual of the Kshatriya castes?

explanation.correct_reasoning: In the Upanayana (sacred-thread) ritual of the Kshatriya varna, the prescribed mantra was the Trishtubh Mantra. Gayatri Mantra is the best-known and is associated with Brahmins — a common distractor here.
Upanayana marked the initiation ('second birth') of the twice-born varnas (dvija).
Trishtubh is a Vedic metre; the association of specific metres with varnas is a ritual-detail fact.

Brahmin=Gayatri, Kshatriya=Trishtubh, Vaishya=Jagati.

en.question_text: Where is the most famous Kailash temple located among the cave temples?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The most famous Kailash temple (Kailasanatha) among the cave temples is located at the Ellora caves in Maharashtra. It is a rock-cut, monolithic temple attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (8th century CE) and is the largest monolithic rock excavation in the world. Elephanta caves are known for the Shiva Trimurti; Kanheri for Buddhist caves near Mumbai.
Ellora (c. 6th–10th century CE) has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves; Cave 16 is the Kailash temple.

en.question_text: Which of the following Vedas was the earliest composition?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas and is considered the earliest composition in the history of Indian literature/religion. It consists of 1,028 hymns (suktas) arranged in 10 mandalas, composed in early Vedic Sanskrit. Hence option A (Rigveda) is correct.
key_concepts: The four Vedas in order: Rigveda (oldest), Samaveda (melodies/chants), Yajurveda (ritual formulas), Atharvaveda (spells, charms, everyday concerns).
Rigveda is divided into 10 mandalas; famous hymns include the Purusha Sukta and Nasadiya Sukta.
The Rigvedic period is called the Early Vedic period (c. 1500–1000 BCE).

Rigveda = oldest Veda; 10 mandalas; Early Vedic period.

en.question_text: What is called Antaranga Sadhana under Ashtanga Yoga?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Under Ashtanga (eight-limbed) Yoga, the Antaranga (internal) sadhana comprises the inner limbs — principally Dharana (concentration, 6th limb), Dhyana (meditation, 7th) and Samadhi (8th), with Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses, 5th) sometimes treated as the bridge. Among the options, Dharana (rendered 'Dharna' in the paper) is the representative Antaranga sadhana. Hence option D is correct.
key_concepts: Ashtanga Yoga (Patanjali): Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama (first four = Bahiranga/external); Pratyahara (5th, bridge); Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi (6th–8th = Antaranga/internal).
Some traditions include Pratyahara in Antaranga; others treat it as the transition between outer and inner yoga.
Niyama (observances) is the 2nd limb (Bahiranga); Pranayama (breath control) is the 4th limb (Bahiranga).
'Dharna' in the option is a variant spelling of Dharana (one-pointed concentration).
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: Antaranga sadhana = inner limbs = Dharana/Dhyana/Samadhi (6th-8th); option D (Dharna/Dharana).
Bahiranga = first four (Yama to Pranayama); Antaranga = last three (Dharana to Samadhi).

en.question_text: Match the following pairs and identify the correct code: Rivers Area of Origin (1) Kaveri (i) Satpura range (2) Sabarmati (ii) Brahmagiri hills (3) Tapti (Tapi) (iii) Mewad hills (4) Damodar (iv) Chota Nagpur Plateau Code: (1) (2) (3) (4)

West-flowing peninsular rivers: Narmada and Tapti.

en.question_text: The Fundamental Duties were inserted into the Constitution on the recommendation of which committee?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Fundamental Duties were inserted into the Constitution (as Part IVA and Article 51A) by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee (1976). en.question_text: Which of the following statements is not correct?

options.text: El Nino is an ocean current, which appears off the Peru coast.
El Nino weakens the Indian Monsoon.
La Nina strengthens the Indian Monsoon.

explanation.correct_reasoning: The statement that is NOT correct is that El Niño occurs every year. El Niño is the periodic warming of the central/eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean that recurs irregularly roughly every 2–7 years (not annually) and typically weakens the Indian monsoon. La Niña (cooling) generally strengthens the Indian monsoon. Hence option C (El Niño occurs every year) is the false statement and is correct for this 'not correct' question.

option_explanations.text: El Nino is an ocean current, which appears off the Peru coast.
El Nino weakens the Indian Monsoon.
La Nina strengthens the Indian Monsoon.

key_concepts: El Niño = warm phase of ENSO (El Niño–Southern Oscillation); appears off Peru/Ecuador around Christmas (hence 'the Christ Child').
During El Niño, the Walker circulation weakens, reducing monsoon rainfall over India (often drought years).
La Niña = cool phase; generally favours a stronger Indian monsoon.
ENSO events are episodic (every few years), not annual — making 'occurs every year' the incorrect statement.
revision_takeaways: Memory hook: El Niño ➜ not every year (every 2–7 years); weakens Indian monsoon. La Niña strengthens it.
For 'not correct' questions, pick the false statement: C.

sources.title: El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian monsoon — IMD / NCERT geography

en.question_text: The BCG vaccine is administered for protection against:

explanation.correct_reasoning: The BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) vaccine is administered for protection against tuberculosis (TB). key_concepts: Polio is prevented by OPV/IPV; measles by MR/MMR vaccine; Hepatitis B by the Hep-B birth dose — none by BCG.

India's Universal Immunisation Programme includes BCG, OPV, Hep-B, pentavalent, rotavirus, MMR/MR, etc.

BCG = Bacillus Calmette-Guérin ➜ TB.

en.question_text: Who among the following was nominated to the Rajya Sabha by the President of India as the 12th member in the year 2024?
