en.question_text: Arrange the following Indian States in descending order of their geographical areas: 1. Rajasthan II. Tamil Nadu III. Maharashtra IV. Karnataka

explanation.correct_reasoning: By area the four states rank Rajasthan (342,239 sq km), Maharashtra (307,713), Karnataka (191,791) and Tamil Nadu (130,058), so the descending order is I, III, IV, II. Rajasthan is India's largest state and Madhya Pradesh, which is not in the list, sits between it and Maharashtra.

option_explanations.reason: This puts Tamil Nadu ahead of Maharashtra and Karnataka, which is the wrong way round.
This places Maharashtra above Rajasthan, but Rajasthan is about 34,000 sq km larger.
Correct: Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu is the true descending order of area.
This brings Rajasthan in third, behind two smaller states, so the order is not descending.

key_concepts: Largest states: Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh
Karnataka 191,791 sq km; Tamil Nadu 130,058 sq km
Area ranking differs from population ranking
revision_takeaways: Rajasthan is first in area but only around eighth in population.

en.question_text: Which of the following islands of India has volcanic origin?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Barren Island is the emergent summit of a volcano in the Andaman Sea and the only confirmed active volcano in India, with eruptions recorded in 1991, 1994-95, 2005 and 2017. The Nicobar and North Andaman islands are part of the same island arc but are not volcanic in origin.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: Barren Island is a volcanic island with a live cone, about 138 km north-east of Port Blair.
Car Nicobar is a flat coral-and-sedimentary island with no volcanic activity.
Little Nicobar is also a non-volcanic island of the Nicobar group, covered in forest and coral terraces.
North Andaman is an uplifted sedimentary island of the Andaman arc, not a volcano.

key_concepts: Barren Island: only active volcano in India, in the Andaman Sea
Narcondam is a dormant volcano in the same arc
Andaman and Nicobar islands lie on the Burma plate margin
revision_takeaways: One volcano in India, and it is Barren: the name does the work.

en.question_text: Among the following, which one is related to Blue Revolution in India?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Blue Revolution refers to the rapid growth of aquaculture and fisheries, that is, fish production, so pisciculture is the match. Floriculture is flower farming, sericulture is silk rearing and horticulture is fruit and vegetable cultivation, each with its own colour-coded revolution in exam usage.

option_explanations.reason: Floriculture is the cultivation of flowers and is linked to the ornamental trade, not to the Blue Revolution.
Sericulture is silk production and has its own colour label, the Golden Revolution being used for horticulture and honey.
Correct: pisciculture, or fish farming, is the core of the Blue Revolution in India.
Horticulture is the Golden Revolution, covering fruits, vegetables and flowers.

key_concepts: Blue Revolution: fisheries and aquaculture
Green Revolution: foodgrains; White: milk; Yellow: oilseeds; Pink: prawn and onion
Fish production is a major export earner for India
revision_takeaways: Blue is for water produce, which means fish, which means pisciculture.

en.question_text: The boundary line between India and Pakistan is an example of

explanation.correct_reasoning: A superimposed boundary is one drawn over an already settled landscape, ignoring the cultural and physical facts on the ground, and the Radcliffe Line of 1947 was drawn in weeks across Punjab and Bengal without regard to communities. An antecedent boundary would predate settlement, a subsequent one would follow it, and a relict boundary is one that has ceased to function.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: the Radcliffe Line was imposed on existing populations by an outside commission, the classic superimposed boundary.
An antecedent boundary is drawn before the area is settled, as in parts of the Americas, which is not the Indian case.
A relict boundary no longer functions as a political line, whereas the India-Pakistan border is very much in force.
A subsequent boundary is drawn after settlement and follows cultural differences, which the Radcliffe Line deliberately did not do.

key_concepts: Boundary types by timing: antecedent, subsequent, superimposed, relict
Radcliffe Line: 17 August 1947 award, drawn by Cyril Radcliffe
Africa's colonial boundaries are the standard example of superimposed lines
revision_takeaways: Drawn over people by outsiders equals superimposed; the Radcliffe Line is the textbook case.

en.question_text: Which of the following coastal areas of India was affected by Hudhud Cyclone?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Cyclone Hudhud came in from the Bay of Bengal and made landfall near Visakhapatnam on 12 October 2014, devastating the north Andhra coast before weakening over Chhattisgarh. Its name was contributed by Oman, and the response in Andhra Pradesh became a benchmark for evacuation.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: Hudhud struck near Visakhapatnam in October 2014 with winds above 170 km per hour.
Kerala lies on the Arabian Sea side and Hudhud never crossed the peninsula to reach it.
Chennai was hit by the 2015 floods and by cyclone Vardah in 2016, not by Hudhud.
West Bengal's storms include Aila and Amphan; Hudhud made landfall far to the south-west.

key_concepts: Bay of Bengal cyclones: Hudhud 2014, Phailin 2013, Amphan 2020
Landfall categories use wind speed; storm surge causes most deaths
Cyclone names come from a rotating list of member countries
revision_takeaways: Hudhud means hoopoe and hit Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, in October 2014.

en.question_text: Which of the following water reservoirs is built on Chambal River?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Rana Pratap Sagar is the dam and reservoir at Rawatbhata on the Chambal, downstream of Gandhi Sagar and upstream of Jawahar Sagar, and it is part of the Gandhi Sagar-Chambal cascade. Nagarjuna Sagar is on the Krishna, Rihand on the Rihand river and Vindhya Sagar is a small MP tank, none of them on the Chambal.

option_explanations.reason: Nagarjuna Sagar stands on the Krishna river in Telangana, one of the earliest large masonry dams of India.
Correct: the dam at Rawatbhata on the Chambal forms the Rana Pratap Sagar reservoir and has a hydropower station.
Vindhya Sagar is a small state reservoir of Madhya Pradesh, not one of the Chambal dams.
Rihand is a reservoir on the Rihand river, a Son tributary, in Uttar Pradesh.

key_concepts: Chambal cascade: Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar, Jawahar Sagar, Kota Barrage
Rana Pratap Sagar is famous for the Rawatbhata atomic power station nearby
Chambal drains the Malwa plateau into the Yamuna
revision_takeaways: Four Chambal dams in order, with Rana Pratap Sagar at Rawatbhata.

en.question_text: Which among the following has the largest shipyard in India?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Cochin Shipyard Limited is the largest shipbuilding and repair facility in India, a public sector yard that also built the Vikrant's hull and repairs the Navy's carriers. Kolkata's Garden Reach and Visakhapatnam's Hindustan Shipyard are significant but smaller, and Mumbai's yards serve port needs.

option_explanations.reason: Kolkata has the Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers, a major yard but not the largest by capacity.
Correct: Cochin Shipyard is India's largest shipbuilding and maintenance facility, at Kochi in Kerala.
Mumbai's yards are mainly repair docks, including the Mazagon Dock, which is known for submarines rather than size.
Hindustan Shipyard at Visakhapatnam is one of the oldest yards but smaller than Cochin in capacity.

key_concepts: Cochin Shipyard: largest Indian yard, public sector, under the Ministry of Shipping
Mazagon Dock builds submarines; Garden Reach builds warships
Shipbuilding is covered under the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Policy
revision_takeaways: Largest shipyard is Cochin, and the second name to know is Garden Reach.

en.question_text: The power plant at Manikaran, based on geothermal energy. is located in the State of

explanation.correct_reasoning: Manikaran lies in the Parvati Valley of Kullu district, Himachal Pradesh, where hot springs are tapped for a small geothermal power plant. The site is also a place of pilgrimage, and the state's geothermal belt runs along the Beas and Parvati valleys.

option_explanations.reason: Arunachal has hot springs at Tawang and Dirang, but its geothermal potential is still exploratory.
Jammu and Kashmir's springs at Puga in Ladakh are promising but Manikaran is far away in Himachal.
Correct: the experimental 5 MW plant at Manikaran is in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu district.
Uttarakhand has Tapovan and Badrinath springs, but not the Manikaran plant.

key_concepts: Geothermal energy: heat from the earth's interior used to raise steam
Manikaran hot springs, Parvati Valley, Kullu
Puga in Ladakh is India's most promising geothermal field
revision_takeaways: Manikaran, Kullu, Himachal Pradesh: the Indian geothermal example.

en.question_text: Badlands of Madhya Pradesh are the result of

explanation.correct_reasoning: The badlands and ravines of the Chambal in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan are cut by deep gullies that retreat headward into soft alluvium, so gully erosion is the process. Sheet erosion removes a thin uniform layer, overgrazing is a contributory cause rather than the mechanism, and wind erosion shapes deserts.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: concentrated runoff carves deep gullies whose headward retreat produces the Chambal ravine badlands.
Sheet erosion strips soil evenly across a slope and does not cut the deep branching channels seen at Chambal.
Overgrazing removes protective vegetation and accelerates erosion, but it is a cause of vulnerability, not the landform process.
Wind erosion dominates arid Rajasthan further west and forms dunes, not the dendritic ravines of the Chambal.

key_concepts: Badland: intensely dissected land unusable for farming
Gully erosion follows uncontrolled runoff on soft, easily erodible alluvium
Chambal ravines are a classic Indian example alongside the Yamuna ravines
revision_takeaways: Ravines are gullies grown up, and the agent is running water.

en.question_text: When was the Central Ganga Authority' established in India?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Central Ganga Authority, later the National Ganga River Basin Authority, was set up in February 1985 to implement the Ganga Action Plan under the Environment Protection Act framework, chaired by the Prime Minister. The 1986 environment law and the 2009 NGRBA are separate, later steps.

option_explanations.reason: 1998 belongs to later river conservation programmes, not the founding of the Ganga authority.
1972 is the year of the Wildlife (Protection) Act and the Stockholm Conference, not the Ganga authority.
2001 is far too late for the body that launched the Ganga Action Plan in 1985.
Correct: the Central Ganga Authority was constituted in 1985 under Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi.

key_concepts: Ganga Action Plan 1985, Phase I and II
NGRBA 2009, chaired by the Prime Minister; Namami Gange launched in 2014
River pollution control is shared between the centre and states
revision_takeaways: Ganga Authority 1985 comes just before the Environment Protection Act of 1986.

en.question_text: Which one of the following States is related with Silent Valley Project?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Silent Valley is a tropical evergreen rainforest in the Palakkad district of Kerala, and the hydroelectric project proposed there in the 1970s was dropped after a national campaign led by the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad. The valley is now a national park and part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve.

option_explanations.reason: Uttarakhand's environmental battles were over the Tehri dam and limestone quarrying, not Silent Valley.
Himachal's controversies centred on hydro projects in the Sutlej valley and on the Great Himalayan National Park.
Correct: Silent Valley in Palakkad district, Kerala, was saved from a hydroelectric project and became a national park.
Tamil Nadu's forests host the Mudumalai sanctuary, but Silent Valley lies across the state border in Kerala.

key_concepts: Silent Valley National Park, Palakkad, Kerala
Saved in 1983 after the Silent Valley Hydro-Electric Project was abandoned
Habitat of the lion-tailed macaque
revision_takeaways: Silent Valley equals Kerala, lion-tailed macaques and a cancelled dam.

en.question_text: Golden Quadrilateral Project of India joins

explanation.correct_reasoning: The Golden Quadrilateral connects the four metropolitan cities Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata in a loop of about 5,846 km, built under the National Highways Development Project. The other options describe north-south or east-west corridors or simply different routes.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: these four metros form the Golden Quadrilateral, the country's first mega highway project.
This is a stretch of the North-South Corridor, a different NHDP programme.
Srinagar to Kolkata is the northern arm of the East-West Corridor, not the quadrilateral.
Porbandar to Kolkata belongs to the East-West Corridor, connecting Gujarat with Bengal.

key_concepts: Golden Quadrilateral: 5,846 km, launched 2001 under NHDP Phase I
North-South Corridor: Srinagar to Kanyakumari; East-West: Porbandar to Silchar
Golden Quadrilateral connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata
revision_takeaways: Four metros in a loop is the Quadrilateral; the corridors run north-south and east-west.

en.question_text: Potato is a

explanation.correct_reasoning: The potato is a modified underground stem, specifically a tuber, because it carries axillary buds in the depressions called eyes and stores starch. Roots bear no buds, bulbs are made of fleshy leaf scales as in onion, and a fruit is the ripened ovary of a flower.

option_explanations.reason: A root has no nodes or buds; the potato's eyes are buds, which shows it is stem tissue.
A fruit develops from the ovary after flowering, whereas the potato is a vegetative storage organ.
Correct: the potato is a stem tuber, a swollen underground stem with nodes and buds.
A bulb, as in onion and garlic, is a short stem surrounded by fleshy scale leaves, which the potato is not.

key_concepts: Stem modifications: tuber, rhizome, corm, bulb
Eyes of the potato are axillary buds used for seed propagation
Solanum tuberosum belongs to the Solanaceae family
revision_takeaways: Bud-bearing underground swelling means stem: potato is a tuber, onion is a bulb.

en.question_text: Which gas is known as 'noble gas?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Helium belongs to group 18 of the periodic table, the noble gases, which are characterised by full outer shells and very low reactivity. Hydrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide are not noble gases, even though hydrogen sits next to helium in the first period.

option_explanations.reason: Hydrogen has one electron and forms compounds readily; despite its position it is not a noble gas.
Oxygen is a highly reactive group 16 element and the basis of combustion.
Correct: helium is a noble gas with a closed 1s2 shell, the least reactive element known.
Carbon dioxide is a compound, not an element, so it cannot be a noble gas.

key_concepts: Noble gases: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon
Full valence shells make noble gases chemically inert
Helium is used in balloons and cryogenics
revision_takeaways: Group 18 is the noble family, and helium is its lightest member.

en.question_text: The largest gland in human body is

explanation.correct_reasoning: The liver is the largest gland in the human body, weighing about 1.5 kg in an adult, and it secretes bile, stores glycogen and detoxifies the blood. The pancreas and salivary glands are much smaller, and the adrenal glands are small endocrine caps on the kidneys.

option_explanations.reason: The pancreas has both digestive and hormonal roles but weighs only about 80 to 100 grams.
Correct: at about 1.5 kg the liver is the largest gland and the largest internal organ.
Salivary glands are small paired glands that secrete saliva into the mouth.
The adrenal glands are tiny caps on top of the kidneys that release adrenaline and cortisol.

key_concepts: Liver: bile secretion, glycogen storage, detoxification
Largest organ is the skin; largest gland is the liver
The liver receives blood through the portal vein
revision_takeaways: Skin is the largest organ, liver the largest gland: keep the two apart.

en.question_text: Mammals respire by

explanation.correct_reasoning: All mammals breathe through lungs, even the whales and dolphins that live in water, since their lungs are supplied by a diaphragm-driven system. Gills belong to fish, the tracheal system to insects, and skin respiration supplements rather than replaces lungs in most mammals.

option_explanations.reason: Gills extract dissolved oxygen from water and are the breathing organs of fish, not of mammals.
Insects breathe through a network of tracheae opening at spiracles, a system mammals do not have.
Skin respiration matters in amphibians and earthworms and only supplementarily in mammals.
Correct: mammals, including aquatic ones, breathe air with lungs.

key_concepts: Respiratory organs: lungs in mammals, gills in fish, tracheae in insects, skin in earthworms
Alveoli provide the surface for gas exchange in mammalian lungs
The diaphragm is unique to mammals
revision_takeaways: Whales breathe air with lungs, which is why the 'lungs' answer covers all mammals.

en.question_text: Vinegar is chemically known as

explanation.correct_reasoning: Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid, roughly 5 per cent, produced by fermenting ethanol with Acetobacter bacteria, so acetic acid is its chemical identity. Butyric acid smells of rancid butter, formic acid is the ant-sting acid and tartaric acid occurs in grapes and tamarind.

option_explanations.reason: Correct: vinegar is ethanoic (acetic) acid, CH3COOH, in water.
Butyric acid gives rancid butter its smell and appears in the digestive tract, not in vinegar.
Formic acid is methanoic acid, found in ant stings and insect venom.
Tartaric acid is the main acid of grapes and tamarind, and it appears in baking powder.

key_concepts: Acetic acid CH3COOH is a weak carboxylic acid
Fermentation: sugar to ethanol to acetic acid
Useful acids: citric (lemon), lactic (curd), oxalic (tomato)
revision_takeaways: Vinegar equals acetic acid, and the everyday acids each have a fixed source.

en.question_text: Myopia is the disorder of which organ?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Myopia, or short-sightedness, is an eye defect in which the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina, so distant objects look blurred and a concave lens is used to correct it. It has no link with the heart, ear or kidney.

option_explanations.reason: Cardiac disorders include hypertension and arrhythmia; myopia is a refractive error of the eye.
Ear disorders affect hearing and balance, such as tinnitus or vertigo.
Correct: myopia is poor distant vision caused by an over-long eyeball or too much lens curvature.
Kidney disease affects filtration and blood pressure, not the refraction of light.

key_concepts: Myopia: image before the retina, corrected with a concave lens
Hypermetropia: image behind the retina, corrected with a convex lens
Presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation
revision_takeaways: Myopia is short sight and needs a concave lens; the organ is always the eye.

en.question_text: Which one of the following is not the unit of heat?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Heat is measured in calories and joules, and the kilocalorie and kilojoule are simply multiples of them. The watt is a joule per second, that is, a unit of power, so it does not measure heat quantity.

option_explanations.reason: A calorie is the classic unit of heat, the energy needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 degree Celsius.
The kilocalorie is 1,000 calories and is the unit used on food labels for energy content.
The kilojoule is the SI-based multiple of the joule, which is itself the SI unit of energy and heat.
Correct as the odd one out: a watt is one joule per second, a rate of energy transfer, so it measures power.

key_concepts: 1 calorie = 4.18 joules
Power = energy per unit time; watt = J/s
Electric heaters are rated in watts because they are power devices
revision_takeaways: Joules and calories are energy; watts are energy per second.

en.question_text: The liquid/liquids used in simple barometer is/are

explanation.correct_reasoning: A simple barometer uses mercury because its high density of 13.6 g per cc keeps the column to about 76 cm at sea level; water would need a tube over 10 m tall and alcohol still higher. That is why mercury is the standard liquid in barometers and manometers.

option_explanations.reason: Water is too light: atmospheric pressure would support a column of more than 10 metres, which is impractical.
Correct: mercury's density allows a manageable 76 cm column, and it does not wet the glass.
Alcohol is less dense than water and also evaporates, so it suits thermometers, not barometers.
Only mercury is used in practice, so a blanket 'all' answer is wrong.

key_concepts: Atmospheric pressure at sea level equals 760 mm of mercury or 101.3 kPa
Mercury barometer, aneroid barometer, altimeter
Torricelli's experiment established the principle in 1643
revision_takeaways: Density is the reason: mercury compresses the column to 76 cm.

en.question_text: Which one of the following is not a fossil fuel?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels formed from buried organic matter over millions of years. Uranium is a radioactive metal mined from rock and used as nuclear fuel, so it is not a fossil fuel.

option_explanations.reason: Coal is compressed plant remains and is the classic fossil fuel.
Petroleum forms from marine organic matter and is refined into petrol, diesel and kerosene.
Natural gas is mostly methane formed alongside oil and coal beds.
Correct: uranium is nuclear fuel obtained by mining and enrichment, not a fossil fuel, though it is also non-renewable.

key_concepts: Fossil fuels are carbon-based remains of ancient life
Uranium-235 undergoes fission in reactors
Both fossil and nuclear fuels are non-renewable, but only the first are fossil
revision_takeaways: Uranium is non-renewable and non-fossil; that distinction is the answer.

en.question_text: Which one of the following is a renewable source of energy?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Solar energy is renewable because it is continuously replenished by sunlight, whereas coal, petrol and nuclear fuel are finite stores that are used up. Solar power is harnessed through photovoltaic panels and solar thermal systems.

option_explanations.reason: Coal took millions of years to form and is depleted once burnt, so it is non-renewable.
Nuclear power depends on mined uranium, a finite resource, so it is not classified as renewable.
Petrol is a refined petroleum product and therefore a fossil fuel.
Correct: sunlight is continuously available and is the leading renewable source.

key_concepts: Renewable sources: solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass
India's solar target of 100 GW by 2022 under the National Solar Mission
Photovoltaic effect converts light directly into electricity
revision_takeaways: Renewable means replenished by nature, not merely clean: nuclear is clean but not renewable.

en.question_text: The formal and real beginning of Five-Year Plans is said to have started in Madhya Pradesh from

explanation.correct_reasoning: The paper dates the formal beginning of economic planning in Madhya Pradesh to 11 November 1956, the year the reorganized state came into being and the Second Five-Year Plan began. Standard MP economy texts instead begin the state's own plan series with the Third Five-Year Plan (1961-66), because the reorganized state's first full plan period was that one, so the question carries two defensible answers.

option_explanations.reason: Many MP economy texts treat 1961-66 as the state's first full plan after reorganization, which is why this option is also defensible.
The Second Plan (1956-61) began the same year as the new state but is not the benchmark either source uses.
The First Plan (1951-56) ran before Madhya Pradesh existed in its present form, so it cannot date state planning.
Keyed answer: the state public service commission and the paper use 11 November 1956 as the date planning formally began.

key_concepts: Madhya Pradesh was reorganised on 1 November 1956
National plans: First 1951-56, Second 1956-61, Third 1961-66
MP State Planning Board was constituted on 24 October 1972
revision_takeaways: Learn the pair: 11 November 1956 per MPPSC, Third Plan per standard MP texts.

dispute.reason: The paper dates the real beginning of economic planning in Madhya Pradesh to 11 November 1956 and keys D, while standard MP economy texts treat the Third Five-Year Plan (1961-66) as the first plan of the reorganised state, which makes A equally defensible.

en.question_text: Starch is a

explanation.correct_reasoning: Starch is a polysaccharide built from hundreds of glucose units joined by alpha-1,4 and alpha-1,6 linkages, which is why it must be broken down by amylase before absorption. Monosaccharides are single sugars such as glucose, and disaccharides are pairs such as sucrose and lactose.

option_explanations.reason: Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides, the simplest sugars with a single ring.
Sucrose, lactose and maltose are disaccharides made of two sugar units.
Correct: starch is a large polymer of glucose, with amylose and amylopectin fractions.
The classification above does apply, so the negative option fails.

key_concepts: Starch: alpha-glucose polymer, digestible by humans
Cellulose: beta-glucose polymer, indigestible by humans
Iodine test turns starch blue-black
revision_takeaways: Starch and cellulose are both glucose polysaccharides; only the linkage differs.

en.question_text: Trophic level-1 includes

explanation.correct_reasoning: Trophic level 1 is the level of the producers, the green plants and algae that capture solar energy and convert it into chemical form. Herbivores form level 2, carnivores level 3 or higher, and omnivores feed across several levels.

option_explanations.reason: Herbivores are primary consumers and sit at trophic level 2, not 1.
Carnivores occupy level 3 or above as secondary and tertiary consumers.
Omnivores feed at several levels and cannot be pinned to level 1.
Correct: green plants are the producers at the base of every food chain.

key_concepts: Energy flows from producers to consumers and is lost as heat at each step
Ten per cent law of energy transfer between trophic levels
Food web versus food chain
revision_takeaways: Level 1 is always the producers; levels count consumers upward from there.

en.question_text: Pasteurization is related to

explanation.correct_reasoning: Pasteurization heats milk, typically to 63 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes or 72 degrees for 15 seconds, and then cools it quickly to kill disease-causing organisms and extend shelf life. It is a heat treatment aimed at making milk safe, which the option calls sterilization of milk, though strictly it is milder than true sterilization.

option_explanations.reason: Correct in the paper's sense: heat treatment of milk to kill pathogens, named after Louis Pasteur.
Dehydration removes water to make milk powder, a different process.
Fermentation uses bacteria to make curd and yoghurt, which pasteurization is designed to prevent.
Distillation separates liquids by boiling point and is not used on milk.

key_concepts: Pasteurization: HTST 72 degrees/15 s and LTLT 63 degrees/30 min
Sterilization needs about 115-120 degrees and kills all microbes, spores included
UHT treatment gives longer shelf life than pasteurization
revision_takeaways: Pasteurization kills pathogens, not all spores; the paper still wants 'sterilization of milk'.

en.question_text: Ozone hole is caused by

explanation.correct_reasoning: The springtime ozone hole over Antarctica forms because chlorine and bromine released from chlorofluorocarbons and halons are catalytically destructive to ozone in the polar stratosphere. Acetylene and ethylene are hydrocarbons and methane is a greenhouse gas without a comparable ozone-destroying cycle.

option_explanations.reason: Acetylene is a fuel gas used in welding and does not carry chlorine into the stratosphere.
Ethylene is a plant hormone and industrial feedstock, and it plays no part in the ozone hole.
Correct: CFCs release chlorine in the stratosphere, and one chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.
Methane is a greenhouse gas and only a minor ozone precursor, not the cause of the hole.

key_concepts: Ozone hole over Antarctica, discovered in the 1980s
Montreal Protocol 1987 phased out CFCs and halons
Polar stratospheric clouds speed the chlorine reaction in the polar spring
revision_takeaways: Ozone hole equals CFCs; the remedy is the Montreal Protocol.

en.question_text: Who among the following environmentalists is known by the name of Jal Purush?

explanation.correct_reasoning: The environmentalist known as Jal Purush, the Waterman of India, is Rajendra Singh of Alwar in Rajasthan, who founded Tarun Bharat Sangh and revived rivers such as the Arvari through johad water harvesting; he won the Magsaysay Award in 2001 and the Stockholm Water Prize in 2015. The option prints his name as Rajendra Choudhary, but the person described by the other clues is unmistakably Rajendra Singh.

option_explanations.reason: Bahuguna led the Chipko movement for Himalayan forests and is not called Jal Purush.
Correct as printed: the option stands for Rajendra Singh, founder of Tarun Bharat Sangh and Waterman of India.
Venkateswarlu is an agricultural scientist associated with dryland farming research, not with this title.
Salim Ali, the Birdman of India, worked on ornithology and had no water conservation role.

key_concepts: Rajendra Singh: johad revival, Arvari river, Tarun Bharat Sangh
Magsaysay Award 2001; Stockholm Water Prize 2015
Johad is a traditional earthen check dam of Rajasthan
revision_takeaways: Jal Purush means Rajendra Singh; the printed surname in this paper is a slip.

en.question_text: Who was the protagonist of Chipko Movement?

explanation.correct_reasoning: Sunderlal Bahuguna is the figure most closely identified with the Chipko movement, which began in Chamoli in 1973 when villagers hugged trees to stop felling, and he coined the slogan that ecology is the permanent economy. Chandi Prasad Bhatt led the Dasholi Gram Swarajya Mandal that launched the first Chipko protests, and Gaura Devi led the Reni village action, so several people share the movement's leadership.

option_explanations.reason: Medha Patkar is associated with the Narmada Bachao Andolan and the Sardar Sarovar dam protests.
Swaminathan is the scientist behind the Green Revolution in India, not an anti-felling agitator.
Correct: Bahuguna is the acknowledged leader and public face of the Chipko movement.
Bhatt co-founded the movement's first organisation in 1973 and is a strong alternative, but the paper credits Bahuguna as protagonist.

key_concepts: Chipko 1973, Chamoli, Uttarakhand: tree hugging against commercial felling
Gaura Devi led the Reni village protest in 1974
Bahuguna's slogan: ecology is the permanent economy
revision_takeaways: Chipko leaders: Bhatt started it, Bahuguna became its voice, Gaura Devi led its most famous action.

dispute.reason: The paper keys Sunderlal Bahuguna as the protagonist of the Chipko movement. Chandi Prasad Bhatt led the Dasholi Gram Swarajya Mandal that organised the first 1973 protests and Gaura Devi led the Reni action of 1974, so the leadership is shared and option D is defensible.

en.question_text: Which of the following institutions is not related with environment?

en.question_text: Which of the following Acts introduced the Principle of Constitutional Autocracy'?

The 1909 and 1919 Acts stopped short of it, and the 1947 Act simply transferred power.

option_explanations.reason: The 1909 Act enlarged the councils and introduced separate electorates, but the executive remained responsible to the Secretary of State, not to a charter-bound autocrat.

option_explanations.text: The Government of India Act of 1919
option_explanations.reason: The 1919 Act brought dyarchy into the provinces and a measure of Indian participation, which is the opposite direction from constitutional autocracy.

option_explanations.text: The Government of India Act of 1935
option_explanations.reason: Correct: the 1935 Act gave Governors and the Governor-General wide overriding powers written into a rigid constitution, the arrangement known as constitutional autocracy.
The 1947 Act wound up British rule and created the dominions, so it cannot be the source of an imperial autocratic principle.

key_concepts: 1935 Act: provincial autonomy, federation, bicameralism, rigid constitution

1935 Act abolished dyarchy in provinces but introduced it at the centre
revision_takeaways: Constitutional autocracy is the phrase reserved for the 1935 Act's Governor-General and Governors.

en.question_text: A batsman hits a cricket ball which then rolls on a level ground. After covering a short distance, the ball comes to rest. The ball slows to a stop because

options.text: the batsman did not hit the ball hard enough
velocity is proportional to the force exerted on the ball
there is a force on the ball opposing the motion
there is no unbalanced force on the ball, so the ball would try to come to rest

explanation.correct_reasoning: Once the bat has hit the ball, gravity and an unbalanced force exist in the rolling friction and air resistance that act opposite to the motion, so the ball decelerates until it stops. Newton's first law says a body keeps moving unless a force opposes it, which is exactly what the friction option states.

option_explanations.text: the batsman did not hit the ball hard enough
option_explanations.reason: How hard the ball is hit changes how far it goes, but it does not explain why any rolling ball eventually stops.

option_explanations.text: velocity is proportional to the force exerted on the ball
option_explanations.reason: Force changes momentum; velocity is not proportional to the applied force in the way this option claims.

option_explanations.text: there is a force on the ball opposing the motion
option_explanations.reason: Correct: friction between ball and ground plus air resistance act opposite to the motion and bring the ball to rest.

option_explanations.text: there is no unbalanced force on the ball, so the ball would try to come to rest
option_explanations.reason: With no unbalanced force the ball would continue at constant velocity forever, so this option inverts Newton's first law.

key_concepts: Newton's first law: uniform motion needs no force
Rolling friction and air resistance oppose motion
Friction converts kinetic energy into heat
revision_takeaways: A body at rest or in uniform motion has zero net force; stopping always requires friction.
